links.outcome: Subgroup accuracy, false positive and false negative rates by nSES and race
links.effect: Accuracy was similar across nSES and racial subgroups, but false positives were higher for low vs high nSES (RR 1.50 [1.44-1.56]) and Black vs White (2.05 [1.92-2.19]); false negatives lower for Black vs White (0.63 [0.59-0.67]).
links.quote: The algorithm assigned more false positives for medication nonadherence among low vs high nSES (RR [95%CI] 1.50 [1.44-1.56]) and Black vs White (2.05 [1.92-2.19]) subgroups.

links.outcome: Whether fairness assessment tied to clinical use case reveals disparity worsening
links.effect: Applied to 3 hypothetical use cases, worsening of disparities was pertinent where false positives could be particularly harmful, e.g., if nonadherence predictions prompted lower treatment priority.
links.quote: When applied to 3 hypothetical use cases, worsening of existing disparities was pertinent for clinical applications where false positives could be particularly harmful (e.g, if predictions of nonadherence prompted lower treatment priority).

links.outcome: Risk flags potentially driving lower treatment priority for groups with more false positives
links.effect: More false positives in low nSES and Black patients could worsen disparities if nonadherence predictions prompted lower treatment priority.
links.quote: When applied to 3 hypothetical use cases, worsening of existing disparities was pertinent for clinical applications where false positives could be particularly harmful (e.g, if predictions of nonadherence prompted lower treatment priority).

screen.reason: Retrospective algorithmic fairness and disparity audit evaluating how predictive performance metrics (false positive/negative rates across racial/SES subgroups) translate across hypothetical clinical use cases.
